## Overview

Latent change score models describe change itself
[@McArdle-2009].
Take vocabulary and reading comprehension measured once a year in children.
From one occasion to the next, each child's vocabulary changes.
In the dual change score model, the change has two sources:
a constant amount each child gains every year (the slope),
and an amount that depends on where the child stood the year before
(the self-feedback).
In the bivariate model, the change in one variable
can also depend on the previous level of the other variable
(the coupling),
for example, if children with a larger vocabulary
gain more in reading comprehension.

The dual change score model is usually fitted
as a structural equation model (SEM).
It can also be written as a state space model:
the true levels of the two variables are latent states,
and the slopes are latent states that never change.

This tutorial does three things:

1. It writes the bivariate dual change score model as a state space model.
2. It simulates data from the model with `SimSSMFixed()`.
3. It fits the model to the simulated data with `dynr` (state space)
   and with `lavaan` (SEM),
   and compares both sets of estimates with the values used to simulate the data.

No prior knowledge of state space models is needed.



## Model

The measurement model is given by
\begin{equation}
  \left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    Y_{1_{i, t}} \\
    Y_{2_{i, t}} \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  =
  \left(
  \begin{array}{cccc}
    1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
    0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  \left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \eta_{1_{i, t}} \\
    \eta_{2_{i, t}} \\
    \eta_{3_{i, t}} \\
    \eta_{4_{i, t}} \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  +
  \left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \varepsilon_{1_{i, t}} \\
    \varepsilon_{2_{i, t}} \\
  \end{array}
  \right),
  \quad
  \mathrm{with}
  \quad
  \left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \varepsilon_{1_{i, t}} \\
    \varepsilon_{2_{i, t}} \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  \sim
  \mathcal{N}
  \left(
  \mathbf{0},
  \left(
  \begin{array}{cc}
    \theta_{11} & 0 \\
    0 & \theta_{22} \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  \right)
\end{equation}
where $Y_{1_{i, t}}$ and $Y_{2_{i, t}}$
are the two observed variables
at time $t$ and individual $i$,
$\eta_{1_{i, t}}$ and $\eta_{2_{i, t}}$ are their true levels,
$\eta_{3_{i, t}}$ and $\eta_{4_{i, t}}$ are their slopes,
and $\theta_{11}$ and $\theta_{22}$
are the measurement error variances.

In words,
each observed score is the true level plus measurement error.
The slopes have loadings of 0:
they affect the scores only through the change in the true levels.

The change in the true level of the first variable
from occasion $t - 1$ to occasion $t$ is
\begin{equation}
  \Delta \eta_{1_{i, t}}
  =
  \eta_{3_{i, t - 1}}
  +
  b_{1} \eta_{1_{i, t - 1}}
  +
  g_{12} \eta_{2_{i, t - 1}} ,
\end{equation}
and similarly for the second variable,
$\Delta \eta_{2_{i, t}} = \eta_{4_{i, t - 1}} + b_{2} \eta_{2_{i, t - 1}} + g_{21} \eta_{1_{i, t - 1}}$.
The true level at occasion $t$ is the previous true level plus the change,
$\eta_{1_{i, t}} = \eta_{1_{i, t - 1}} + \Delta \eta_{1_{i, t}}$.

Writing the change into the level gives the dynamic structure
\begin{equation}
  \left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \eta_{1_{i, t}} \\
    \eta_{2_{i, t}} \\
    \eta_{3_{i, t}} \\
    \eta_{4_{i, t}} \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  =
  \left(
  \begin{array}{cccc}
    1 + b_{1} & g_{12} & 1 & 0 \\
    g_{21} & 1 + b_{2} & 0 & 1 \\
    0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
    0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  \left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \eta_{1_{i, t - 1}} \\
    \eta_{2_{i, t - 1}} \\
    \eta_{3_{i, t - 1}} \\
    \eta_{4_{i, t - 1}} \\
  \end{array}
  \right) .
\end{equation}

In words,
$b_{1}$ and $b_{2}$ are the self-feedback effects:
a negative value means that individuals who stand higher
gain less, so the levels level off over time.
$g_{12}$ is the coupling from the second variable to the first:
a positive value means that a higher level of the second variable
is followed by a larger gain in the first.
$g_{21}$ is the reverse.
The slopes stay the same over time.
As in most applications of the model,
there is no process noise:
once the initial levels and the slopes are set,
the true trajectories are fixed.

The initial condition holds the means, variances, and covariances
of the initial true levels and the slopes,
\begin{equation}
  \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, 0}
  \sim
  \mathcal{N}
  \left(
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\eta} \mid 0},
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\eta} \mid 0}
  \right) .
\end{equation}

For example, a positive covariance between the initial level
and the slope of the same variable means that individuals who start higher
also tend to gain more each year.

### Diagrams



![Path diagram of the dual change score model.](fig-vignettes-lcs-path.png){width=100%}

The bivariate dual change score model as a path diagram, for the first three occasions.
The true level at each occasion, $\eta_{1}$ or $\eta_{2}$, is the previous level plus the latent change $\Delta \eta_{1}$ or $\Delta \eta_{2}$ (the arrows with a loading of 1).
Each change is the slope ($\eta_{3}$ or $\eta_{4}$), plus the self-feedback effect ($b_{1}$ or $b_{2}$) of the previous level of the same variable, plus the coupling effect ($g_{12}$ or $g_{21}$) of the previous level of the other variable.
$\varepsilon_{1}$ and $\varepsilon_{2}$ are the measurement errors.
The initial levels and the slopes all covary; to keep the diagram readable, only $\sigma_{12}$, $\sigma_{13}$, $\sigma_{24}$, and $\sigma_{34}$ are drawn.

![State space form of the dual change score model.](fig-vignettes-lcs-ssm.png){width=100%}

The same model in state space form.
All the latent variables at one occasion form the state vector $\boldsymbol{\eta}_{t}$, and all the observed variables form $\mathbf{y}_{t}$.
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$ carries the state from one occasion to the next, $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ maps the state to the observed variables, and $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ is the covariance matrix of the measurement error $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{t}$.
The latent changes are not states: writing each change into the level gives the first two rows of $\boldsymbol{\beta}$.
There is no process noise.
`SimSSMFixed()` takes `beta`, `lambda`, and the Cholesky factor of $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ (`theta_l`);
`psi_l` is a matrix of zeros.

## Data Generation

### Notation

Let $t = 6$ be the number of time points and $n = 10000$ be the number of individuals.

Let the self-feedback effects be $b_{1} = -0.2$ and $b_{2} = -0.3$,
and the coupling effects be $g_{12} = 0.1$ and $g_{21} = 0.2$,
so that

\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{\beta}
=
\left(
\begin{array}{cccc}
  0.8 & 0.1 & 1 & 0 \\
  0.2 & 0.7 & 0 & 1 \\
  0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
  0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
\end{array}
\right) .
\end{equation}

Let the initial condition be

\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\eta} \mid 0}
=
\left(
\begin{array}{c}
  2 \\
  1 \\
  0.5 \\
  0.4 \\
\end{array}
\right)
\quad \mathrm{and,} \quad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\eta} \mid 0}
=
\left(
\begin{array}{cccc}
  1 & 0.3 & 0.15 & 0.05 \\
  0.3 & 1 & 0.05 & 0.15 \\
  0.15 & 0.05 & 0.25 & 0.05 \\
  0.05 & 0.15 & 0.05 & 0.25 \\
\end{array}
\right) ,
\end{equation}

and the measurement error variances be
$\theta_{11} = 0.2$ and $\theta_{22} = 0.2$.

### R Function Arguments

The simulation functions take covariance matrices
as lower triangular Cholesky factors (the arguments ending in `_l`).
There is no process noise, so `psi` and `psi_l` are zero matrices.


``` r

time

mu0

sigma0

sigma0_l # sigma0_l <- t(chol(sigma0))

psi
```

### Visualizing the Dynamics Without Measurement Error (n = 5 with Different Initial Condition)

Without measurement error,
each individual's true levels follow smooth curves
that bend as the self-feedback slows the gains.

<img src="fig-vignettes-lcs-no-error-lcs-1.png" alt="" width="3300" /><img src="fig-vignettes-lcs-no-error-lcs-2.png" alt="" width="3300" />

### Using the `SimSSMFixed` Function from the `simStateSpace` Package to Simulate Data

Now we add the measurement error and simulate the full data set.
`as.data.frame()` returns the data in long format,
one row per individual and time point,
with the columns `id`, `time`, `y1`, and `y2`.


``` r
library(simStateSpace)
sim <- SimSSMFixed(
  n = n,
  time = time,
  mu0 = mu0,
  sigma0_l = sigma0_l,
  alpha = alpha,
  beta = beta,
  psi_l = psi_l,
  nu = nu,
  lambda = lambda,
  theta_l = theta_l,
  type = 0
)
data <- as.data.frame(sim)
head(data)
#>   id time       y1           y2
#> 1  1    0 1.239124 -0.034741096
#> 2  1    1 2.372287 -0.050275519
#> 3  1    2 2.550748 -0.363167146
#> 4  1    3 3.417814 -0.164406246
#> 5  1    4 3.685087  0.007406512
#> 6  1    5 3.473986 -0.348501993
summary(data)
#>        id             time           y1               y2         
#>  Min.   :    1   Min.   :0.0   Min.   :-4.626   Min.   :-5.4249  
#>  1st Qu.: 2501   1st Qu.:1.0   1st Qu.: 1.474   1st Qu.: 0.8794  
#>  Median : 5000   Median :2.5   Median : 2.462   Median : 1.8642  
#>  Mean   : 5000   Mean   :2.5   Mean   : 2.543   Mean   : 1.9673  
#>  3rd Qu.: 7500   3rd Qu.:4.0   3rd Qu.: 3.524   3rd Qu.: 2.9522  
#>  Max.   :10000   Max.   :5.0   Max.   :10.947   Max.   :10.9199
plot(sim)
```

## Model Fitting

We first fit the model with `dynr`,
which estimates state space models by maximum likelihood
using the Kalman filter.

A `dynr` model is built from pieces that match the equations above:
the data, the initial condition, the measurement model,
the dynamic model, and the noise.
Each parameter gets a name (for example, `g_1_2` for $g_{12}$),
and the same name used in two places means one shared parameter.
The starting values are set to the population values for convenience;
with real data, they would be rough guesses.

### Prepare Data

Tell `dynr` which columns hold the individual, the time, and the observed variables.


``` r
dynr_data <- dynr::dynr.data(
  dataframe = data,
  id = "id",
  time = "time",
  observed = c("y1", "y2")
)
```

### Prepare Initial Condition

The means, variances, and covariances
of the initial true levels and the slopes are all estimated.


``` r
dynr_initial <- dynr::prep.initial(
  values.inistate = mu0,
  params.inistate = c("mu0_1_1", "mu0_2_1", "mu0_3_1", "mu0_4_1"),
  values.inicov = sigma0,
  params.inicov = matrix(
    data = c(
      "sigma0_1_1", "sigma0_2_1", "sigma0_3_1", "sigma0_4_1",
      "sigma0_2_1", "sigma0_2_2", "sigma0_3_2", "sigma0_4_2",
      "sigma0_3_1", "sigma0_3_2", "sigma0_3_3", "sigma0_4_3",
      "sigma0_4_1", "sigma0_4_2", "sigma0_4_3", "sigma0_4_4"
    ),
    nrow = 4
  )
)
```

### Prepare Measurement Model

The loadings are fixed.


``` r
dynr_measurement <- dynr::prep.measurement(
  values.load = lambda,
  params.load = matrix(data = "fixed", nrow = 2, ncol = 4),
  state.names = c("eta_1", "eta_2", "eta_3", "eta_4"),
  obs.names = c("y1", "y2")
)
```

### Prepare Dynamic Process

The first two formulas read as
"the new true level is the previous level plus the change",
with the change made of the slope, the self-feedback, and the coupling.
The slopes carry over unchanged.


``` r
dynr_dynamics <- dynr::prep.formulaDynamics(
  formula = list(
    eta_1 ~ eta_1 + eta_3 + b_1 * eta_1 + g_1_2 * eta_2,
    eta_2 ~ eta_2 + eta_4 + b_2 * eta_2 + g_2_1 * eta_1,
    eta_3 ~ eta_3,
    eta_4 ~ eta_4
  ),
  startval = c(
    b_1 = b_1, b_2 = b_2,
    g_1_2 = g_1_2, g_2_1 = g_2_1
  ),
  isContinuousTime = FALSE
)
```

### Prepare Process Noise

The process noise is fixed at zero,
and the two measurement error variances are estimated.


``` r
dynr_noise <- dynr::prep.noise(
  values.latent = psi,
  params.latent = matrix(data = "fixed", nrow = 4, ncol = 4),
  values.observed = theta,
  params.observed = matrix(
    data = c(
      "theta_1_1", "fixed",
      "fixed", "theta_2_2"
    ),
    nrow = 2
  )
)
```

### Prepare the Model

The pieces are put together into one model.
`dynr` writes the model as C code to `outfile` and compiles it.


``` r
model <- dynr::dynr.model(
  data = dynr_data,
  initial = dynr_initial,
  measurement = dynr_measurement,
  dynamics = dynr_dynamics,
  noise = dynr_noise,
  outfile = "lcs.c"
)
```

The plot below shows the model equations with the parameter names.

<img src="fig-vignettes-lcs-model-lcs-1.png" alt="" width="3300" />

### Fit the Model


``` r
results <- dynr::dynr.cook(
  model,
  debug_flag = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

## The Dual Change Score Model in Structural Equation Modeling

The same model in SEM form, fitted with `lavaan`,
should give nearly the same estimates.
In SEM, each variable at each occasion is a separate observed variable
in one row per individual (wide format).
Each observed score has a true-level factor;
each true level after the first is the previous true level
plus a change factor;
and each change factor is the slope
plus the self-feedback and coupling effects.

### Wide Data Set

`as.data.frame()` with `long = FALSE` returns the data in wide format.


``` r
data <- as.data.frame(sim, long = FALSE)
head(data)
#>   id     y1_0       y2_0     y1_1        y2_1     y1_2        y2_2     y1_3
```

### Model

The model has the same structure for every occasion,
so we write it with `paste0()`.
The parameter labels match the dynr names.
Giving the self-feedback and coupling effects
and the measurement error variances the same label on every occasion
constrains them to be equal over time,
as in the state space model.


``` r
waves <- 0:(time - 1)
now <- waves[-1]
before <- waves[-time]
model <- paste(
  c(
    "# true levels",
    paste0("l1_", waves, " =~ 1 * y1_", waves),
    paste0("l2_", waves, " =~ 1 * y2_", waves),
    "# each true level is the previous level plus the change",
    paste0("l1_", now, " ~ 1 * l1_", before),
    paste0("l2_", now, " ~ 1 * l2_", before),
    paste0("l1_", now, " ~~ 0 * l1_", now),
    paste0("l2_", now, " ~~ 0 * l2_", now),
    paste0("d1_", now, " =~ 1 * l1_", now),
    paste0("d2_", now, " =~ 1 * l2_", now),
    "# the change: self-feedback and coupling",
    paste0("d1_", now, " ~ b_1 * l1_", before, " + g_1_2 * l2_", before),
    paste0("d2_", now, " ~ b_2 * l2_", before, " + g_2_1 * l1_", before),
    paste0("d1_", now, " ~~ 0 * d1_", now),
    paste0("d2_", now, " ~~ 0 * d2_", now),
    "# the change: slopes",
    paste0("s1 =~ ", paste0("1 * d1_", now, collapse = " + ")),
    paste0("s2 =~ ", paste0("1 * d2_", now, collapse = " + ")),
    "# initial true levels and slopes: means",
    "l1_0 ~ mu0_1_1 * 1",
    "l2_0 ~ mu0_2_1 * 1",
    "s1 ~ mu0_3_1 * 1",
    "s2 ~ mu0_4_1 * 1",
    "# initial true levels and slopes: variances and covariances",
    "l1_0 ~~ sigma0_1_1 * l1_0",
    "l2_0 ~~ sigma0_2_2 * l2_0",
    "s1 ~~ sigma0_3_3 * s1",
    "s2 ~~ sigma0_4_4 * s2",
    "l1_0 ~~ sigma0_2_1 * l2_0",
    "l1_0 ~~ sigma0_3_1 * s1",
    "l1_0 ~~ sigma0_4_1 * s2",
    "l2_0 ~~ sigma0_3_2 * s1",
    "l2_0 ~~ sigma0_4_2 * s2",
    "s1 ~~ sigma0_4_3 * s2",
    "# measurement error variances, equal over time; no observed intercepts",
    paste0("y1_", waves, " ~~ theta_1_1 * y1_", waves),
    paste0("y2_", waves, " ~~ theta_2_2 * y2_", waves),
    paste0("y1_", waves, " ~ 0 * 1"),
    paste0("y2_", waves, " ~ 0 * 1")
  ),
  collapse = "\n"
)
cat(model)
```

so every parameter above is exactly the one written.

## Table of Parameters and Estimates

The table below puts each population value used to simulate the data
next to its estimate.
Bias is the estimate minus the population value.
Because the model is fitted to a single simulated data set,
this is the error of one estimate, not a Monte Carlo bias,
which would average over many replications.
The 95% confidence interval is the Wald interval,
$\hat{\theta} \pm 1.96 \times \mathrm{SE}$,
and `Covers` shows whether it contains the population value.


``` r
EstimatesTable <- function(population, estimate, se) {
  z <- stats::qnorm(p = 0.975)
  ll <- estimate - z * se
  ul <- estimate + z * se
  data.frame(
    Parameter = names(population),
    Population = unname(population),
    Estimate = unname(estimate),
    SE = unname(se),
    Bias = unname(estimate - population),
    `2.5%` = unname(ll),
    `97.5%` = unname(ul),
    Covers = unname(population >= ll & population <= ul),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}
```


``` r

  mu0_1_1 = mu0[1],

  g_2_1 = g_2_1,
  theta_1_1 = theta[1, 1],
  theta_2_2 = theta[2, 2]
)
```

``` r
se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(results)))

  x = EstimatesTable(
    population = population,
    estimate = estimates,
    se = se[names(population)]
  ),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Population values and dynr estimates (one simulated data set)"
)
```

``` r
pe <- lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit)
# a label shared by several occasions is one parameter
pe <- pe[pe$label != "" & !duplicated(pe$label), ]
rownames(pe) <- pe$label
knitr::kable(
  x = EstimatesTable(
    population = population,
    estimate = pe[names(population), "est"],
    se = pe[names(population), "se"]
  ),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Population values and lavaan estimates (one simulated data set)"
)
```
